title: Exclusive: Paying for frontier AI models buys 4-month head start at 5x the cost
gist: Mozilla's second State of Open Source AI report finds the capability gap between US closed frontier models and the best Chinese open-weights models has narrowed to 4.4 months, with Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 scoring within three points of Anthropic's Fable 5 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 30 percent of the cost. The practical upshot is that closed models only earn their ~5x per-task premium on a narrow band of 8-to-12-hour tasks, expert professional work, high-intensity retrieval and long context — and Mozilla CTO Raffi Krikorian warns that the world's open-model commodity layer is now funded almost entirely by Chinese capital.

insights.claim: The performance gap between US frontier AI models and the best Chinese open-weights models has narrowed to just 4.4 months, according to Mozilla's State of Open Source AI report published September 15, 2026.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A sub-half-year capability lead means closed-model pricing power decays on a quarterly clock — model the frontier premium as a depreciating asset, not a moat.
insights.quote: The performance gap between frontier AI models from US tech companies and the best open-weights models from Chinese companies has closed to just 4.4 months
insights.locator: Opening paragraph

insights.claim: Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 scores just three points behind Anthropic's Fable 5 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index composite while costing only 30 percent as much.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A 70 percent cost saving for three index points is the arbitrage driving enterprise model mix shift — expect closed-model gross revenue per token to compress.
insights.locator: The report highlights how a leading open model

insights.claim: Paying for closed frontier models buys roughly a four-month head start at about five times the per-task cost, and only for tasks in the eight-to-twelve-hour band.
insights.speaker: Raffi Krikorian
insights.so_what: This is the cleanest available formulation of the closed-model value proposition — if a buyer's workload sits outside that band, the 5x premium is pure waste.
insights.quote: paying for closed frontier models buys about a four-month head start at about five times the per-task cost—but only when currently looking at tasks taking between eight and 12 hours.
insights.locator: In other words, paying for closed frontier models

insights.claim: Mozilla's CTO argues most organizations should use open models as the default for the majority of their work, reserving closed models for specific workloads rather than adopting one vendor organization-wide.
insights.speaker: Raffi Krikorian
insights.so_what: A workload-specific rather than organization-specific buying frame breaks vendor lock-in economics and favors routing/gateway layers over single-model contracts.
insights.quote: We see the decision to pay for closed [models] as workload-specific rather than organization-specific.
insights.locator: Raffi Krikorian, chief technology officer at Mozilla

insights.claim: Closed models earn their premium in exactly three places: expert professional work, high-intensity retrieval, and long context.
insights.speaker: Raffi Krikorian
insights.so_what: These three niches define the defensible revenue pool for frontier labs — companies whose AI spend falls outside them are churn candidates.
insights.quote: [A Closed model] earns its premium in a few places: expert professional work, high-intensity retrieval, and long context
insights.locator: Raffi Krikorian, chief technology officer at Mozilla, said in an email

insights.claim: Krikorian's buying rule is to pay for closed models only when the head start is worth it — such as a deadline landing before the open frontier catches up — because routine ongoing work will be doable for a fifth the cost soon and the model will not be the bottleneck anyway.
insights.speaker: Raffi Krikorian
insights.so_what: Reframes frontier AI spend as buying time rather than capability, which caps willingness to pay at the value of a four-month schedule pull-forward.
insights.quote: Routine work you’ll still be doing next quarter is not, because you’ll be able to do it for a fifth of the cost soon, and the model won’t be the bottleneck anyway.
insights.locator: Pay when that head start is worth it

themes.theme: METR time horizons as the capability yardstick

insights.claim: The research nonprofit METR defines a model's 'time horizon' as the length of task — measured by how long human experts need — that the model can complete with a reliable 50 percent success rate, and that horizon has been doubling on a cadence that has accelerated over time.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Task-duration doubling is a cleaner leading indicator for AI labor substitution than benchmark scores — track METR releases as the cadence variable in adoption models.
insights.locator: the research nonprofit METR has defined an AI model's time horizon

insights.claim: The best closed model can currently handle a job 1.7 times as long as the longest job the best open model can reliably finish.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A 1.7x ratio quantifies the frontier lead in task-duration terms — narrow enough that one open-model release cycle erases it.
insights.locator: The best closed model can currently do a job that is 1.7 times as long

insights.claim: Krikorian projects that in four months the open frontier will handle the 12-hour job that closed models handle today, while the closed frontier moves to roughly 20 hours.
insights.speaker: Raffi Krikorian
insights.so_what: A dated, falsifiable forecast — if open models hit 12 hours by early 2027, enterprise spend rotates hard toward self-hosted inference and away from API contracts.
insights.quote: If the open frontier can handle a seven-hour job, the closed frontier can handle a 12-hour one
insights.locator: If the open frontier can handle a seven-hour job

insights.claim: No model of either type can reliably complete tasks longer than 12 hours, while tasks under eight hours can be done by either type and should be routed to cheaper open models.
insights.speaker: Raffi Krikorian
insights.so_what: The 12-hour ceiling caps today's realistic automation scope and defines how much of a knowledge-work task graph AI can actually absorb this cycle.
insights.locator: Tasks requiring between eight and 12 hours are typically the ones

insights.claim: Closed frontier models ship with lab-built harnesses — the software layer giving models tool access and memory for agentic actions — which can inflate their measured performance relative to how the same models perform on third-party harnesses.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Headline benchmark leads may be harness artifacts rather than model capability — discount vendor-published evals that do not control for scaffolding.
insights.locator: closed frontier models often come with their own harness

insights.claim: When benchmarking company Vals AI ran every model on the same neutral harness in Terminal-Bench 2.1, the open-weights GLM 5.2 from Chinese company Z.ai scored within a point of Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.7 and 4.8 while costing about five times less per completed task.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Harness-controlled parity at one-fifth the cost is the strongest single data point for closed-model margin compression in agentic coding workloads.
insights.locator: To level the playing field, benchmarking company Vals AI

themes.theme: Why enterprises still pay for closed models

insights.claim: Organizations keep paying for closed frontier models because they work out of the box and bundle compliance packaging, support, and accountability, while many organizations lack the staff to run open-weights models well.
insights.speaker: Raffi Krikorian
insights.so_what: The remaining moat is operational and legal, not technical — which is monetizable by managed open-model providers, not just by frontier labs.
insights.locator: Organizations still pay for closed frontier models because they work out of the box

insights.claim: DoorDash runs Kimi for routine work while reserving Fable for harder tasks that would normally take human experts longer, a live example of tiered model routing by workload difficulty.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A named large-enterprise reference for splitting spend across Chinese open and US closed models — evidence the mix shift is real, not theoretical.
insights.locator: For example, delivery company DoorDash has been using Kimi for routine work

insights.claim: Open-weights models release downloadable model components but developers typically withhold training data, the data pipeline, and training code, so 'open weights' is materially less open than open source software.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: The distinction matters for regulated buyers and for auditability claims — do not treat open-weights availability as equivalent to supply-chain transparency.
insights.locator: The open-weights AI models allow anyone to download the main model components

insights.claim: Eight of the top ten models by token volume on the AI gateway OpenRouter in August 2026 provide open weights.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Token-volume share is where substitution shows up first; OpenRouter rankings are a public, high-frequency proxy for the mix shift before it hits vendor revenue.
insights.locator: The surging popularity of open-weights models can be seen on OpenRouter

insights.claim: A Linux Foundation paper by Frank Nagle and Daniel Yue found open models captured just 4 percent of model revenue against 96 percent for closed models, though the data covered only May through September 2025.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Token share and revenue share have decoupled — the monetization gap is the key uncertainty in sizing open models as a threat to frontier lab P&Ls.
insights.locator: A paper by Frank Nagle and Daniel Yue for the Linux Foundation

insights.claim: Krikorian expects the 96/4 closed-to-open revenue split to have already shifted because open models have exploded in the year since that data was collected.
insights.speaker: Raffi Krikorian
insights.so_what: If revenue share follows token share with a lag, frontier lab revenue growth rates are the number to stress-test in 2027 forecasts.
insights.quote: In the last year, open models have exploded, so we do expect revenue to have shifted
insights.locator: In the last year, open models have exploded

insights.claim: Adoption of open models accelerated between Mozilla's inaugural report on July 14, 2026 and the September 15 edition, a measurable shift inside a two-month window.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Two-month observable acceleration suggests the substitution curve is steep enough to matter within a single earnings cycle.
insights.locator: this has accelerated the use of open models since Mozilla's inaugural

themes.theme: Chinese capital owns the commodity layer

insights.claim: Most of the open models the world runs on are Chinese, and Chinese labs are running the same playbook Americans ran with Android — give the product away but own the surrounding ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Raffi Krikorian
insights.so_what: If the Android analogy holds, the value accrues to whoever controls defaults, tooling and distribution around free models — not to the model weights themselves.
insights.quote: The Chinese labs are running the same playbook the Americans ran with Android—give it away, but own the ecosystem around it
insights.locator: The current reality is that most of the open models the world runs on are Chinese

insights.claim: The plural open-weight AI ecosystem is largely funded by Chinese capital, which Krikorian describes as a plurality and a concentration at the same time.
insights.speaker: Raffi Krikorian
insights.so_what: Open-model diversity is a single-country dependency in disguise — a policy and supply risk for Western enterprises standardizing on Chinese weights.
insights.quote: The uncomfortable truth is that the plural ecosystem around open-weight AI is largely funded by Chinese capital right now
insights.locator: The uncomfortable truth is that the plural ecosystem

insights.claim: Krikorian's stated concern is concentration rather than Chinese models per se: the best open models are concentrated in China while the best closed frontier models come from US companies, and he wants US and European labs competing in the same open lane so no single country sets the world's defaults.
insights.speaker: Raffi Krikorian
insights.so_what: Frames a policy argument likely to shape Western public funding for open models — a potential new demand source for compute and a competitive threat to closed labs.
insights.locator: But Krikorian is not so concerned about Chinese models

themes.theme: Blueprint for a Western open-model coalition

insights.claim: Krikorian argues the Linux precedent shows how an alternative coalition could form: open source infrastructure was funded by organizations that each needed the commodity layer to exist, plus neutral foundations.
insights.speaker: Raffi Krikorian
insights.so_what: Identifies the funding mechanism for a non-Chinese open frontier — watch for consortium formation among firms whose economics depend on cheap commodity models.
insights.locator: The history of development for open source software like Linux

insights.claim: Such a coalition would be made of institutions with a mission rather than a market — public compute programs funding fully open reference models, neutral foundations extending internet-protocol governance into models and agentic standards, beneficiary companies, and philanthropy covering evaluation and audit infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Raffi Krikorian
insights.so_what: Maps four distinct funding pools for open AI infrastructure; the evaluation-and-audit gap is explicitly flagged as commercially unfunded, i.e. a whitespace.
insights.quote: institutions with a mission rather than a market
insights.locator: Any coalition for building more open AI models would likely consist of

insights.claim: Switzerland's national compute program producing the Apertus model is cited as a working example of public compute funding fully open reference models.
insights.speaker: Raffi Krikorian
insights.so_what: Sovereign compute programs are an emerging non-commercial buyer of GPUs and a template other governments may copy — incremental, policy-driven accelerator demand.
insights.locator: Switzerland's national compute producing Apertus is an example.

insights.claim: Krikorian argues open-weights is not sufficient for trust because it is hard to fully trust a model with decisions when you cannot tell how it was trained or what it was evaluated against.
insights.speaker: Raffi Krikorian
insights.so_what: Training-data and eval transparency is the next battleground for regulated-industry AI procurement — a differentiator neither Chinese open labs nor US closed labs currently offer.
insights.quote: It’s hard to fully trust a model with decisions if you can’t tell how it was trained or what it was evaluated against
insights.locator: Krikorian also called for the alternative coalition to go even further
